16.purpose: This slide explains how we compare training masks fairly. If each model were tested on a different pattern of missing joints, a performance difference could reflect the question we asked rather than what the model learned.
16.explanation: We therefore give Random U, Whole joint J and Anatomical A the same saved test masks. Scattered hiding (U bank) removes observations throughout the window. Grouped hiding E_leg deliberately removes neighboring lower-leg observations together, making nearby joints less available as clues. These are two distinct completion tasks, and each is evaluated separately.
16.visual: Read across each training-method row. Every method is tested on both scattered and grouped hiding, using the saved masks for each task. Within either column, the same physical targets and mask draws support the comparison, rather than a fresh random test for each method.
16.evidence: Both banks contain 16 masks, each hiding 64 of 128 tokens. Grouped hiding E_leg balances left and right legs and four temporal starts, and scores only the eight deliberately grouped tokens in each mask. The stored banks make these comparisons reproducible. Matching the number hidden does not make the two tasks equally difficult.
16.transition: With the evaluation questions fixed, the next slide identifies which parts of model fitting change across the three training methods and which parts remain shared.

17.purpose: This slide locates the masking experiment within the model. It tests how different missing-observation patterns train the corrections, while preserving a common starting prediction for every comparison.
17.explanation: The Own-leg baseline f is trained with Random U and then kept fixed. For each masking policy, the Own-leg correction f+h learns from the target leg, while the Both-leg correction f+g can also use the opposite leg. Normal-only internal validation selects regularization and correction size. Separate random streams prevent a mask choice from unintentionally changing the source sampling schedule.
17.visual: The first card identifies the shared baseline, the second identifies the matched comparisons, and the third explains separate random streams. A drawn mask can hide measurements that were already invalid, so equal masking budgets need not produce identical numbers of usable training targets. The saved support counts show that difference.
17.evidence: The two corrections each have 154 features and the same output dimension. Their recorded numerical ranks differ, so equal width does not establish equal effective flexibility. This completed comparison concerns coordinate predictors. It does not demonstrate an optimal JEPA encoder mask, and the separate JEPA experiment has its own training recipe.
17.transition: The next slide checks whether these fitted corrections work adequately on normal development recordings before we interpret their behavior on held-out recordings.

18.purpose: Before using a cross-leg prediction as a measurement, we need evidence that the model can make useful predictions. This development check asks whether the Both-leg correction f+g improves on sensible local alternatives.
18.explanation: Within each outer training set, three internal folds hold out normal recordings in turn. The selected both-leg recipe must improve on the Own-leg baseline f and the Own-leg correction f+h in at least two of those three folds, with improvement in the average validation loss as well. Abnormal labels do not choose these settings.
18.visual: Each point summarizes one outer fold and training policy. Positive values mean that the Both-leg correction f+g has lower validation error than the Own-leg correction f+h. The point plot shows one part of the check; the saved gate also compares against the baseline.
18.evidence: All 12 combinations of four outer folds and three masking policies pass the declared development rule. These are checks after model selection on the same development folds, so they are not independent test results. Passing permits evaluation; it cannot guarantee a benefit on every recording or observation pattern.
18.transition: We now move from normal development data to the held-out normal recordings and examine how the prediction benefit changes between scattered and grouped hiding.

19.purpose: This slide asks the central completion question on held-out normal recordings: after using the target leg, how much does the fitted model gain from also using the other leg?
19.explanation: Benefit is the error of the Own-leg correction f+h minus the error of the Both-leg correction f+g on the same hidden target. A positive value means that the both-leg prediction is more accurate. We calculate that difference for Random U, Whole joint J and Anatomical A under each fixed evaluation bank.
19.visual: First compare the three methods within Scattered hiding (U bank), then within Grouped hiding E_leg. Read the interval beside each mean, rather than ranking methods from the means alone. An interval crossing zero leaves the direction of the benefit uncertain under this analysis.
19.evidence: All 28 held-out normal recordings contribute to each result. On scattered hiding, the Random U and Anatomical A intervals include zero. All three grouped-hiding intervals are positive. Removing neighboring leg observations together makes opposite-leg context more useful to these fitted predictors, although the two banks ask different questions and their absolute errors are not interchangeable.
19.transition: The next slide makes these predictions concrete by showing one saved coordinate patch alongside its measured target, before we return to the aggregate completion results.

20.purpose: This example connects the numerical experiment to an actual movement measurement. It lets us inspect what the three predictors produce for the same hidden patch instead of treating an error value as an abstract result.
20.explanation: The observed target is a four-sample block from BlazePose joint 25, the left knee. The Own-leg baseline f predicts it from permitted target-leg observations. The Own-leg correction f+h adjusts that prediction using additional own-leg features, while the Both-leg correction f+g can also use opposite-leg observations. Every comparison retains the same target and body reference.
20.visual: Follow each predicted trace against the observed coordinate trace. The plotted coordinates use the experiment's body-centered, torso-scaled representation, so their values are not distances in meters. The accompanying source identifiers allow the corresponding video and pose overlay to be opened in notebook 13.
20.evidence: This is the saved example from source 3KnFt8bH3tE, sequence cljo2wwu7001a3n6ljmqm39l6, joint 25 and patch 1. It was selected deterministically by source and target order, not by the largest improvement. One patch helps audit coordinate order and target identity, but it does not estimate typical accuracy.
20.transition: Having seen an individual prediction, we can now summarize completion gains across the normal recordings and the independent laboratory participants without mistaking this example for the overall result.

41.purpose: The two results here show where opposite-leg context improves completion across groups of held-out observations. They compare the Both-leg correction f+g with the Own-leg correction f+h, rather than comparing two training masks.
41.explanation: In GAVD, Random U training reduces mean normal-recording error by 19.5% on Grouped hiding E_leg. In the laboratory data, the corresponding reduction is 5.2% across 128 held-out healthy participants. Each percentage divides the difference between group mean errors by the own-leg comparator's mean error. It is not an average of individual percentage improvements.
41.visual: Read the two results separately. GAVD predicts torso-scaled image coordinates, whereas the laboratory study predicts processed joint angles in degrees. The percentages communicate relative improvement within each study; the underlying error values should not be pooled across these measurement systems.
41.evidence: The GAVD absolute benefit is 0.015748, with conditional 95% interval [0.010721, 0.021300]. The laboratory relative interval is [3.6%, 6.7%], calculated after outcome inspection from frozen predictions. Neither interval includes retraining uncertainty. Different feature ranks also mean these gains establish useful fitted predictor families, rather than isolate a capacity-free neurological relationship.
41.transition: The next slide asks a different question: using the same both-leg predictor design and evaluation targets, with the correction weights refitted, does Anatomical A training improve completion compared with Random U training?

43.purpose: This comparison tests the training mask itself. Both sides use the Both-leg correction f+g, so the question is whether Anatomical A training prepares that model better than Random U training for a particular missing-observation task.
43.explanation: On Grouped hiding E_leg, mean error decreases from 0.065020 with Random U to 0.060009 with Anatomical A. That is a 7.7% reduction, with a conditional 95% interval from 6.4% to 9.0%. On Scattered hiding (U bank), the reduction is only 0.8%, with an interval from -1.0% to 2.6%.
43.visual: Use zero as the reference for the two relative-improvement estimates. The grouped-hiding interval stays above zero, while the scattered-hiding interval crosses it. The pattern supports matching training to a specific kind of missing context, rather than expecting the same advantage everywhere.
43.evidence: The paired audit verifies matching sources, physical targets and evaluation masks across the two training methods. On grouped hiding, 27 of 28 recordings improve. These intervals were calculated after inspecting saved outcomes and are descriptive, with models held fixed. The result concerns coordinate completion, not a new masking family, neurological mechanism or demonstrated anomaly-detection gain.
43.transition: To examine anomaly detection, we next turn prediction benefit into a separate cross-leg score and explain how it is combined with directly observed movement.

21.purpose: Accurate completion and anomaly detection answer different questions. This slide explains how the study turns observed movement and cross-leg prediction benefit into separate recording-level anomaly scores.
21.explanation: Movement M measures how unusual the visible posture and movement are. Its 16 video measurements describe knee posture, ankle travel, changes in movement speed, trunk tilt and side differences. Cross-leg R asks a different question: is the improvement from seeing the other leg unusual compared with separate normal reference recordings? Either an unusually large or unusually small improvement can increase R.
21.visual: Read the first two cards as separate measurements. M describes the visible movement. R describes how much the opposite leg helps predict a hidden part of movement, compared with the normal reference. The third card adds these two scores and divides by two to form S. The weights stay fixed rather than being selected to improve the test results.
21.evidence: M learns its reference from fitting-normal recordings. R uses five different normal recordings reserved until after model selection. For each target leg, R subtracts the normal mean benefit, scales the difference by estimated normal variation, and squares it; the final score averages the two legs. This reference scaling does not produce a probability of disease. Five recordings give an uncertain estimate, and equal weights do not guarantee equally reliable score scales.
21.transition: Before comparing these scores, the next slide explains how repeated predictions become one recording-level result and how the evaluation avoids counting correlated windows as independent evidence.

22.purpose: A recording can generate many overlapping windows and masked predictions, but those predictions do not create new independent people. This slide explains the aggregation and uncertainty calculations used to evaluate the anomaly scores.
22.explanation: We first average prediction errors and benefits across repeated masks of the same physical target, then aggregate targets, windows and sequences into recording-level measurements while retaining the declared joint weights. AUROC then measures how often an abnormal recording receives a higher anomaly score than a normal recording. We calculate it within each fold and weight folds by their numbers of normal-abnormal pairs.
22.visual: Follow the measurement hierarchy toward a single recording score before reading the ranking step. This avoids giving a long or heavily sampled video extra influence merely because it supplies more windows. The resampling step keeps every method's score for a recording together.
22.evidence: Detection intervals use 1,000 paired bootstrap resamples within fold and label group, with the original fold weights fixed. They condition on the saved fitted models and selected analysis. They exclude retraining variation and cannot resolve unknown repeated people across uploads. Average precision is also reported with each fold's abnormal fraction, because that fraction affects its interpretation.
22.transition: With the recording-level evaluation defined, the next slide compares Movement M and Combined S on the main four-condition group and the broader collection of abnormal folders.

23.purpose: This slide reports whether adding Cross-leg R to Movement M improves the ranking of abnormal recordings. It keeps the detection question separate from the positive completion results we have already examined.
23.explanation: In the main group of 90 recordings, Movement M reaches AUROC 0.694 and Combined S reaches 0.576. This group contains normal recordings and the four requested condition families. Across all 304 retained recordings, treating every non-normal folder as abnormal, the corresponding values are 0.707 and 0.631. Higher AUROC means more accurate ranking under these dataset labels.
23.visual: Compare the two score columns within each row. Both rows show the same direction: the fixed average performs less well than movement alone. The broader row reuses the main group's recordings, so it is a wider population analysis rather than a second independent dataset.
23.evidence: Both comparisons use the same frozen source scores, and prediction-based scores use Scattered hiding (U bank). The study remains exploratory, and folder labels are not independently verified diagnoses. These findings concern the specified cross-leg score and fixed combination. They do not imply that opposite-leg information is useless for completion or for every possible detector.
23.transition: The next slide examines paired uncertainty around these differences, so we can distinguish a measured direction from a small change that the current data cannot resolve.

24.purpose: Point estimates summarize the saved test results, while paired intervals show how much those differences vary when recordings are resampled. This slide puts the key score comparisons on a common difference scale.
24.explanation: For Combined S minus Movement M, a negative value favors movement alone. The main GAVD difference is -0.118, with a conditional 95% interval from -0.217 to -0.025. The broad difference is -0.076, with interval [-0.143, -0.009]. The third row compares Anatomical with Random training for the same combined score on the main group.
24.visual: Use the vertical zero line to interpret each bar. The two combination comparisons lie below zero. The Anatomical A minus Random U detection comparison crosses zero, even though its point estimate is positive. That uncertainty is compatible with several directions of effect; it does not establish equivalence.
24.evidence: The detection intervals use 1,000 paired resamples of recordings while keeping fitted models and original fold weights fixed. Multiple comparisons remain exploratory and unadjusted. The two GAVD rows share recordings, so the plot should not be read as independent confirmations.
24.transition: We next examine all three training-mask detection results together, preserving the same scattered-hiding evaluation task and the distinction between a higher point estimate and an established advantage.

25.purpose: This slide shows the complete training-mask comparison for anomaly detection under Scattered hiding (U bank). Keeping all three policies visible prevents the largest point estimate from becoming a stronger conclusion than the uncertainty supports.
25.explanation: For the main four-condition group, Combined S reaches AUROC 0.576 with Random U, 0.620 with Whole joint J and 0.631 with Anatomical A. The broad results are 0.631, 0.644 and 0.672. Every row uses the same evaluation masks, recording population and score formula; the correction training policy is the factor being compared.
25.visual: Read down one population column at a time. Anatomical A has the largest displayed point estimate, but the table alone does not show whether its advantage is established. Relate it to the paired interval from the preceding slide rather than interpreting row order as a ranking of proven methods.
25.evidence: The main Anatomical A minus Random U difference is 0.055, with conditional interval [-0.018, 0.127]. The other pairwise masking intervals also cross zero. These detection comparisons therefore do not establish a masking advantage, even though the separate grouped completion task shows a clear anatomical-training benefit.
25.transition: The next slide changes the evaluation question to Grouped hiding E_leg and explains why its detection values must be interpreted as a separate diagnostic comparison.

26.purpose: Grouped hiding E_leg tests what happens when neighboring lower-leg observations disappear together. This slide carries that distinct observation task through to anomaly scoring without treating it as interchangeable with scattered hiding.
26.explanation: The main-group Combined S AUROCs are 0.668 for Random U, 0.668 for Whole joint J and 0.684 for Anatomical A. These scores are calculated from grouped targets. Each policy uses a grouped-task normal reference estimated from the same reserved recording identities, because the typical prediction benefit changes when the available context changes.
26.visual: Compare rows within this table to assess training policies on the grouped task. Do not subtract a row from the scattered-hiding table and call the result a pure training improvement. Changing banks changes hidden targets, permitted context and the reference distribution used by Cross-leg R.
26.evidence: All 304 retained recordings support this diagnostic, including the 90-recording main group. Positive normal completion benefits therefore coexist with these separate detection results. The anatomical point estimate remains below Movement M's 0.694 in the main group, and the grouped task does not establish an anomaly-detection advantage over movement alone.
26.transition: We now broaden the comparison to inexpensive movement and prediction-error baselines, which help determine whether a more elaborate relational measurement adds useful detection information.

27.purpose: A new anomaly measurement needs comparison with practical alternatives that use the same test recordings. This slide places the cross-leg combination beside simpler movement, waveform and prediction-error approaches.
27.explanation: Movement M reaches main-group AUROC 0.694, while the movement-plus-baseline-error score reaches 0.700. That score averages M with a normal-referenced distance derived from the Own-leg baseline f's error; it does not simply add raw error. Richer movement features reach 0.677, timing and waveform features reach 0.588, and Isolation Forest reaches 0.551. Combined S with Random U reaches 0.576.
27.visual: Read each row as another way to rank the same recordings. Keep the movement-plus-baseline-error score visible: Movement M is a strong comparator, but it is not the largest point estimate in every comparison. The small difference between 0.700 and 0.694 should not be described as a demonstrated statistical gain.
27.evidence: These anomaly models fit or estimate references using normal recordings only. The complete results also retain own-leg-improvement, correction-error and recording-condition controls. The timing descriptors summarize waveforms; they are not a validated physiological phase measure. These distinctions matter when deciding what a score actually measures.
27.transition: The next slide examines the adapted published pose model, explaining both its measured result and the implementation differences that limit comparisons with the original publication.

28.purpose: Including a published pose-based anomaly method adds a useful reference, provided we explain exactly what was run. This slide reports the STG-NF adaptation used with the available GAVD skeletons and missing measurements.
28.explanation: STG-NF learns a distribution of pose sequences and can score observations that depart from normal training data. Here, the authors' implementation is adapted to the 16-joint graph, and missing values are replaced with medians estimated from fitting-normal recordings. Each fold uses 128 training updates. The comparison preserves the same eligible recordings as the other methods.
28.visual: Compare the adapted STG-NF row with Movement M and Combined S in each population column. Its AUROCs are 0.376 for the main group and 0.435 for the broad group. These values describe this specific fitted adaptation and training budget, rather than the best performance the published method could achieve.
28.evidence: All four folds complete, and the upstream revision and adaptations are recorded. Only five normal recordings have fully complete poses, so an unmodified complete-case analysis cannot use the same split. The result supports a transparent implementation comparison, but not a state-of-the-art claim or a general judgment about normalizing-flow methods.
28.transition: The next slide turns to a separate supervised question: whether learned JEPA features help distinguish the five gait-label groups when condition labels are available for classifier training.
